documents.title: ISHLT consensus statement on donor heart selection

chunks.content: Nonstandard Abbreviations and Acronyms HT heart transplant OPTN Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network Clinical Perspective What Is New? In a national cohort of >4500 pediatric heart transplants, elevated peak donor troponin (>0.66 ng/mL, ≥75th percentile) was independently associated with a higher risk of 1‐year graft loss, whereas donor troponin trends over time were not linked to adverse outcomes. What Are the Clinical Implications? Incorporating peak troponin thresholds into donor assessment, while avoiding unnecessary delays for serial troponin testing may improve organ use and reduce pediatric donor heart discard rates without compromising outcomes. Pediatric patients awaiting heart transplant (HT) experience a higher wait‐list mortality rate than other solid organ transplant recipients. Despite this, the donor discard rates for HT recipients are incredibly high (≈40%). There are multiple reasons why donor hearts are discarded. These include donor age, size, sex, cardiac abnormalities (left ventricular hypertrophy, left ventricular dilation, left ventricular dysfunction, other structural abnormalities), prolonged donor arrest time, and other systemic comorbidities. , One such reason for donor discard has been an elevated donor troponin level. The concern by the transplant clinicians is rooted in earlier studies on this topic that have highlighted the association of elevated donor troponin level and poor outcomes following HT. , , More recently, there have been a few adult studies that have demonstrated that elevated donor troponin values are not associated with worse post‐HT outcomes. , , Among adult studies, investigators have evaluated either last donor troponin value or peak donor troponin value. , There are only 2 older pediatric studies that have evaluated the association between donor troponin value and post‐HT outcomes. , The first study was conducted ≈30 years ago (1991–1994), while the second study was completed >15 years ago (2007–2009). Both these studies used the last available donor troponin value. A recent editorial highlighted that perhaps evaluating the effects of troponin trajectories on post‐HT outcomes would be more informative, as those are the data that clinicians clinically use when making determination for donor acceptance. This study intends to bridge these important knowledge gaps. The primary aim of this study was to evaluate the associations of both peak donor troponin (0 to <25th, 25th to <75th, and ≥75th percentile) and donor troponin trends (increasing, persistently high, persistently low, decreasing) with survival among pediatric patients undergoing HT. The secondary aims were to evaluate the characteristics of donors on the basis of their peak troponin values and troponin trends and to evaluate the characteristics of recipients of these donor organs. Methods Anonymized data and materials are available through request from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) registry. Study Cohort This was a retrospective cohort study using data from the OPTN). The OPTN data system includes data on all donor candidates, waitlisted candidates, and transplant recipients in the United States. Pediatric (aged <18 years at listing) heart‐alone recipients transplanted between January 1, 2007, and June 30, 2020, were included. Analyses are based on OPTN data as of March 11, 2022. Deceased donor information was collected for all heart transplants performed during the study period. Data collection on donor troponin values began December 11, 2006; hence, this study included recipients with donor troponin values beginning in 2007. A total of 82.1% (n=4572) of donors had at least 1 troponin I value. More than 2 troponin I values were recorded for 3256 (71.2%) donors (Figure ). The OPTN data set received by the investigators was deidentified, and therefore this project did not require institutional review board approval. Donor Troponin For the analysis, donor troponins were examined by looking at peak donor troponin values and donor troponin trends over time. Donor troponin I values ≤0.04 ng/mL were considered normal. Peak Donor Troponin The percentiles for peak donor troponin values were calculated using the entire data set of donors with available troponin I values. Specifically, the 25th and 75th percentile cutoffs were derived from the distribution of peak values among all donors. This methodology was used because it provides a more accurate representation of data distribution that is not normally distributed and therefore reduces bias from extreme values. Based on peak donor troponin I values, 3 groups were formed: Donors with troponin values between 0 and the <25th percentile. Donors with troponin values between the 25th and <75th percentiles. Donors with troponin values between 75th and 100th percentiles. Donor Troponin Trends Based on the initial and final donor troponin I values, 4 groups were formed (Table ). Donor Troponin Trends Based on the initial and final donor troponin I values, 4 groups were formed (Table ). The 20% threshold was chosen on the basis of prior literature assessing troponin trends in myocardial infarction, where a 20% change is often considered clinically significant for the detection of myocardial injury. , Statistical Analysis To summarize recipient and donor characteristics, median and interquartile range were used for continuous variables, and counts and percentages were used for categorical variables. To test for differences among groups, ANOVA (for normally distributed) or Kruskal–Wallis (for nonnormally distributed) tests were used for continuous variables after testing for normality via the Shapiro–Wilk test, and χ 2 tests were used for categorical variables. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure , , was used to adjust for multiple comparisons. Unadjusted Kaplan–Meier models for 1‐year probability of graft survival (death or retransplant) were stratified by (1) peak donor troponin and (2) donor troponin trends. These were assessed overall by log‐rank tests of significance. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards model of graft survival was evaluated adjusting for recipient and donor characteristics. The recipient and donor variables were chosen a priori (recipient variables: age, race, primary underlying diagnosis, bilirubin, albumin, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, insurance, and infection requiring intravenous drug therapy 2 weeks before transplant; donor variables: donor age, ischemic time, donor cause of death, donor–recipient height ratio, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), and estimated glomerular filtration rate), , along with the predictors of interest: peak donor troponin I and trends in donor troponin I (increasing, decreasing, persistently high, and persistently low). The proportional hazards assumption was tested along with multicollinearity of variables. The largest percentage of missingness was noted for recipient total serum albumin at transplant (4.1%), followed by donor LVEF (2.0%). Multiple imputation was performed, with 10 imputations for each model data set. , Results Initial and Peak Donor Troponin I Values Of 4572 donors with reported troponin I values, the majority (67.7% [3097/4572]) had abnormal values (>0.04 ng/mL; Figure ). Comparing Recipient Characteristics and Donor Characteristics by Peak Donor Troponin I Values Of 4572 donors, 1226 (26.8%) had peak troponin values between 0 and the <25th percentile, 2210 (48.3%) had values between the 25th and <75th percentiles, and 1136 (24.8%) had values above the 75th percentile. Recipients of donors with peak troponin value above the 75th percentile were more likely than those with values of 0 to <25th percentile and 25th to <75th percentile to be aged 11 to 17 years (47.1% versus 22.9% versus 33.1%), have underlying dilated cardiomyopathy (41.4% versus 36.0% versus 37.8%) or retransplant (6.2% versus 4.2% versus 4.8%), have an implantable cardioverter‐defibrillator (12.8% versus 5.5% versus 8.2%) and higher creatinine and bilirubin values at transplant ( P <0.05 for all; Table ). Donors with peak troponin value above the 75th percentile were more likely than those with values of 0 to <25th percentile and 25 to <75th percentile to be older (median age, 13 versus 3 versus 7 years), boys (64.7% versus 59.2% versus 59.5%), White race (55.5% versus 50.3% versus 52.4%), die from anoxia (48.9% versus 33.5% versus 41.1%), receive cardiopulmonary resuscitation (63.3% versus 44.3% versus 53.7%), and have a LVEF ≤55% (8.7% versus 4.2% versus 6.4%) ( P <0.05 for all; Table ). Comparing Recipient Characteristics and Donor Characteristics by Donor Troponin Trends Of 4572 donors, 445 (9.7%) had increasing, 1738 (38%) had persistently high, 406 (8.9%) had decreasing, and 666 (14.6%) had persistently low donor troponin values. Recipients of donors with increasing or persistently high donor troponin values were more likely than those with decreasing or persistently low values to be aged 11 to 17 years (44.0% versus 38.3% versus 32.5% versus 25.8%), have dilated cardiomyopathy (40.2% versus 39.4% versus 33.5% versus 35.4%), have an implantable cardioverter‐defibrillator (9.7% versus 10.2% versus 7.1% versus 5.7%), and have higher creatinine and bilirubin levels ( P <0.05 for all). Recipients of donors with increasing troponin values were most likely on intravenous inotropes (53.7%; P =0.045; Table ). Donors with increasing or persistently high troponin values were more likely than those with decreasing or persistently low values to be older (median age, 12 versus 10 versus 5 versus 3 years) and have a LVEF ≤55% (7.2% versus 7.9% versus 3.4% versus 3.5%; P <0.05 for all). Also, donors with persistently high troponin values were most likely to have died from anoxia (46.8%), have the lowest estimated glomerular filtration rate, and were most likely to have received cardiopulmonary resuscitation (60.8%) (Table ). Unadjusted Survival Peak Donor Troponin Value The 1‐year unadjusted graft survival (93.0% versus 92.1% versus 92.1%) was not significantly different for recipients transplanted with donors whose peak troponin values were 0 to <25th percentile, 25 to <75th percentile, and ≥75th

Also, donors with persistently high troponin values were most likely to have died from anoxia (46.8%), have the lowest estimated glomerular filtration rate, and were most likely to have received cardiopulmonary resuscitation (60.8%) (Table ). Unadjusted Survival Peak Donor Troponin Value The 1‐year unadjusted graft survival (93.0% versus 92.1% versus 92.1%) was not significantly different for recipients transplanted with donors whose peak troponin values were 0 to <25th percentile, 25 to <75th percentile, and ≥75th percentile ( P =0.572) (Figure ). Also, the 1‐year unadjusted graft survival was not significantly different for recipients with cardiomyopathy (96.7% versus 95.8% versus 96.2%) or congenital heart disease (90.0% versus 88.6% versus 86.2%) when transplanted with donors whose peak troponin values were 0 to <25th percentile, 25 to <75th percentile, and ≥75th percentile ( P =0.702 and P =0.148, respectively; Figures and ). Donor Troponin Trends The 1‐year unadjusted graft survival (91.7% versus 92.5% versus 91.8% versus 93.8%) was not significantly different for recipients transplanted with donors with increasing, persistently high, persistently low, and decreasing donor troponin values ( P =0.497; Figure ). Adjusted Survival In the adjusted analysis, significant recipient risk factors for graft loss in the first year following HT were congenital heart disease (hazard ratio [HR], 2.98), retransplant (HR, 3.14), pretransplant extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (HR, 3.36), public insurance (HR, 1.31), intravenous drug therapy 2 weeks before transplant (HR, 1.59) and lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (Table ). Significant donor risk factors for graft failure included donor cause of death due to cerebrovascular disease or stroke (HR, 1.62). After adjusting for other covariates, peak donor troponin I value was significantly associated with increased post‐HT graft loss (HR, 1.22 [95% CI, 1.00–1.47]; P =0.045; Figure ). In the adjusted analysis, donor ejection fraction was not significantly associated with post‐HT graft loss (HR, 0.85 [95% CI, 0.74–1.01]; P =0.065). Also, compared with recipients of donors with persistently low troponin values, there were no differences in post‐HT graft loss for those with decreasing troponin values (HR, 1.40 [95% CI, 0.88–2.23]), increasing troponin values (HR, 1.40 [95% CI, 0.88–2.21]), or persistently high troponin values (HR, 1.32 [95% CI, 0.91–1.90]; Table ). Discussion Our large study comprehensively assessing the impact of peak donor troponin and donor troponin trends on post‐HT graft survival has several important findings: 1. The majority of donors accepted for pediatric HT had abnormal troponin values. 2. Donors with higher troponin values were older and more likely died from anoxia, received cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and had lower LVEF. 3. Recipients of donors with higher troponin values were also older and more likely to have liver and renal dysfunction. 4. After adjusting for confounders, higher peak donor troponin was associated with an increased risk of graft loss in the first year following HT; there was no association between donor troponin trends and graft loss following HT. Pediatric HT recipients are currently facing a high waitlist mortality rate and have an unacceptably high donor discard rate (≈40%). , It is therefore critically important that an intentional attempt is made to ensure the majority of waitlisted patients undergo HT while reducing donor discard. Over the years, numerous reasons for donor discard have been identified. These include donor age, size, sex, cardiac abnormalities (left ventricular hypertrophy, left ventricular dilation, left ventricular dysfunction, and other structural abnormalities), prolonged donor down time, and other systemic comorbidities. , More recent studies have highlighted that most of the historical reasons for donor discard are in fact not associated with worse outcomes currently. This study evaluated one such important reason for donor discard: donor troponin values. It is well recognized that elevated troponin is a biomarker of myocardial damage and is associated with an increased mortality rate among patients with acute myocardial infarction, myocarditis/pericarditis, heart failure, and following cardiopulmonary bypass. , , , In the field of HT, studies have shown that donor brain death leads to a massive surge in sympathetic activity, cellular injury and apoptosis, release of proinflammatory cytokines, microvascular dysfunction, coronary spasm, and myocardial ischemia, ultimately leading to release of troponin and left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction. , Earlier adult studies have demonstrated that elevated donor troponin is often associated with early graft failure, rejection, and graft loss after HT. , More recent adult studies have challenged the prior notion demonstrating that donor troponin levels were not associated with increased risk for adverse post‐HT outcomes. , There are only 2 pediatric studies to date on this topic. The first study was almost 3 decades ago and evaluated only 19 donors. They found that among 8 donors with elevated cardiac troponin I values, 5 (63%) experienced graft failure. The first study was almost 3 decades ago and evaluated only 19 donors. They found that among 8 donors with elevated cardiac troponin I values, 5 (63%) experienced graft failure. The second study is also more than a decade old and included information for 657 donors. This study evaluated only the last available troponin value and found no association between the final troponin values and graft failure. In a clinical setting, the 2 factors more often deliberated on are the peak donor troponin value and, more importantly, the trend of these values over time. Often, clinicians ask that donor troponin values be repeated to ensure that there is improvement, with the assumption that this correlates with recovery of the myocardium following the event that led to the donor’s demise. An important finding from our national study that evaluated over 4500 donors is that after adjusting for donor and recipient confounders, peak donor troponin value does affect graft outcome for pediatric HT recipients. As noted in this study, recipients of donor hearts with peak troponin levels at the 75th percentile (0.66 ng/mL) exhibited a 22% increased risk of graft loss within the first year after HT compared with recipients of donor hearts with troponin levels at the 25th percentile (0.04 ng/mL). These findings suggest that HT clinicians should exercise caution when considering donor hearts with peak troponin concentrations exceeding 0.66 ng/mL. It is important to mention that, in this study, after adjusting for all other confounders, ejection fraction was not a significant contributor to worse post‐HT graft survival. These findings are similar to a previous multicenter analysis among adult HT recipients, where the authors found that recipients receiving donor hearts with borderline ejection fraction (40%–50%) or reduced ejection fraction (<40%) had similar 1‐year survival to recipients who received donor hearts with normal ejection fraction (≥50%). In this study, post‐HT graft survival for recipients of donors with increasing or persistently high donor troponin values were similar to those with low or decreasing values over time. The authors did not have information as to when the troponin values were collected relative to the time of brain death. It is known that catecholamine levels are highest in the first hour after brain death, and this is when cardiac contractility is most often impaired. , Hence, it is valuable for donor hospitals to collect troponin values at this time, as that may be reflective of peak values that clinicians can then use as they consider donor organ acceptance. Other important findings of this study are the donor and recipient characteristics associated with an elevated troponin. As has been shown in the adult study, we also found donors with elevated troponin to more likely have received cardiopulmonary resuscitation. However, in contrast with the adult study, in our study, donors with elevated troponin levels were more likely to have associated left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Pediatric programs tend to accept donors with elevated troponins for recipients who are sicker, and this may partly be due to the concerns for accepting such donors for otherwise stable recipients. This finding contrasts with adults, where such donors are accepted for patients who are not sicker. We did not find any association between donor troponin trends and graft outcomes. More specifically, post‐HT graft survival for donors with increasing or persistently high donor troponin values were similar to those with low or decreasing values over time. The study findings will be valuable to clinicians and reduce the time and effort by organ procurement organizations, as they often must delay donor operating room time as they are trying to obtain and report repeat troponin values at the recipient institution’s request. Limitations This study has inherent limitations secondary to the use of a national registry for research. It is important to note that, in our study, most pediatric recipients (93.6%) accepted for HT had normal left ventricular function. Given the low number of patients with left ventricular systolic dysfunction, we were unable to determine if an elevated or rising troponin value in those with systolic dysfunction may lead to worse outcomes. We suspect that the reason why left ventricular systolic dysfunction was not a significant risk factor for post‐HT death is the time course of the dysfunction early after brain death. We suspect that the reason why left ventricular systolic dysfunction was not a significant risk factor for post‐HT death is the time course of the dysfunction early after brain death. Left ventricular systolic dysfunction occurring early after brain death may not significantly affect post‐HT outcomes, but if it remains persistently low despite donor optimization, caution will need to be exercised in accepting such hearts. We included only pediatric patients who ultimately underwent HT. HT clinicians thoroughly assess donor–recipient suitability before acceptance. Hence, no comments could be made for donors with elevated troponin who ultimately were not accepted on the basis of this analysis. Conclusions Most pediatric recipients receive hearts from donors with abnormal troponin values. Donors with elevated troponin are more likely to have received resuscitation and have lower left ventricular systolic function. Recipients who receive donor hearts with elevated troponins are often sicker than those who receive donor hearts with normal troponin values. Higher peak donor troponin values (>0.66 ng/mL) were significantly associated with worse 1‐year post‐HT graft survival. However, after adjusting donor and recipient characteristics, neither a persistently elevated donor troponin value nor an increasing donor troponin value leads to worse post‐HT outcomes. Further research is needed to understand the impact of elevated troponins in those with persistent left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Sources of Funding None. documents.title: ISHLT 2023 guidelines for mechanical circulatory support

chunks.content: 1 Introduction The left ventricular assist device (LVAD) is a life-saving therapeutic option for patients with advanced heart failure (HF) [ , ]. According to the latest ISHLT Guidelines for Mechanical Circulatory Support [ ], there are two major indications for mechanical circulatory support: bridge to cardiac transplantation (BTT) or permanent therapy for end-stage refractory heart failure, referred to as destination therapy (DT). Advancements in technology, have led to improved patients outcomes [ ], resulting in increased utilization of LVAD, even as DT [ , ]. The prevalence of HF in adults, coupled with the growing geriatric population, has led to an increased demand for LVAD therapy in this patient group [ ]. A study using data from the National Inpatient Sample in the United States demonstrated a rise in LVAD implantation incidence from 3.5% to 10.5% over a 10-year period in patients aged 75 years and above [ ]. Geriatric patients often have extensive medical histories, significant comorbidity, and disabilities, and malnutrition is highly prevalent in those with HF [ ]. There is a vicious cycle between HF and malnutrition. The development of HF involves hormonal dysregulation, neurohormonal and inflammatory activation, leading to an imbalance between anabolism and catabolism. This imbalance is compounded by increased metabolic demands, reduced appetite, and physical limitations that hinder nutritional intake. Gastrointestinal issues associated with HF medications and the disease itself can further impede nutrient absorption. Dietary restrictions, such as limitations on sodium intake, often result in a lack of nutritional variety, increasing the risk of deficiencies. Malnutrition can drive HF progression, and malnourished individuals with HF experience higher rates of hospitalization, longer recovery times after LVAD implantation, and increased risk of mortality [ , , ]. The geriatric nutritional risk index (GNRI), which incorporates height, weight, and serum albumin, has been validated as a screening tool for malnutrition risk in patients aged 75 years and above [ , ]. Previous studies have found that malnutrition risk, as assessed by GNRI, is associated with a worse prognosis in HF patients [ , , ]. However, there is limited data on the malnutrition risk assessed by GNRI in HF patients aged 75 years and above undergoing LVAD implantation. Our study aims to investigate the relationship between the malnutrition risk, as determined by GNRI values, and outcome of geriatric HF patients undergoing LVADs using data from the Interagency Registry for Mechanically Assisted Circulatory Support (INTERMACS) registry (available at: http://www.intermacs.org ). 2 Patients and methods 2.1 Data source and ethical considerations Data of patients aged over 65 who received LVAD implantation between 2008 and 2017 were retrospectively retrieved from the INTERMACS database, including the relative data of quality of life (QoL) of survivors, as defined by the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) and the 6-minute walk test (6MWT). The INTERMACS is a prospective registry of patients with mechanical circulatory device support. The data for this study were requested through the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Biologic Specimen and Data Repository Information Coordinating Center of the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute ( https://biolincc.nhlbi.nih.gov/home/ ) (approval date: 2021-09-07, application number: #10242). According to the INTERMACS database, the QoL and 6MWT were examined pre-implant, 3 months follow-up, 6 months follow-up, and every 6 months thereafter the LVAD implantation until the device is explanted or the patient has a transplant [ ]. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University (2021-410-02). Patients were excluded if they had age less than 65 years old, with total artificial heart, an isolated right ventricular assist device, a history of ventricular assist device or heart transplantation, or a non-continuous-flow LVAD were excluded. Besides, patients lacking information on gender, height, weight, and serum albumin or those with a history of hepatitis or liver dysfunction were also excluded. The detailed patient selection process is described in . For women, IBW (kg) was calculated by = h e i g h t c m - 100 - ( h e i g h t - 150 / 2 ) . If the patient’s body weight/IBW ≥ 1, then the ratio of weight/IBW was assigned to 1. Patients thus were stratiﬁed into three groups according to the GNRI values: absence of risk: GNRI of ≥98; mild risk: GNRI of 92 to < 98; moderate to severe risk: GNRI of < 92. The primary outcome is long-term survival, up to four years post-implant of LVAD implantation. The secondary outcomes include 1): adverse events including bleeding, cardiac arrhythmia, stroke, infection, right HF, and venous thromboembolism according to the definition of INTERMACS. 2): In survivors, the quality of life (QoL), as defined by the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) and the 6-minute walk test (6MWT). 2.2 Statistical analysis Quantitative and categorical variables are presented as frequency (percentage) and mean ± standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range, IQR) as appropriate. Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests were used to verify the distribution of data. Continuous variables were compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test or one-way ANOVA, while discrete variables were compared using Fisher's exact test or chi-square test, as appropriate. The association of pre-implant and post-implant malnutrition risk with outcomes was investigated as both categorical and continuous variables. Pre-implant malnutrition risk was indicated by GNRI before LVAD implantation, and post-implant malnutrition risk was assessed by GNRI at 6 months after LVAD implantation and time-varying GNRI from 6 months to 4 years after LVAD implantation. For the primary outcome of mortality, Kaplan-Meier analysis, Log-Rank test, Cox regression model, and the adjusted Cox regression model were used to determine differences in survival among groups. Besides, a restricted cubic spline (RCS) Cox proportional hazard regression model was performed to assess the dose-response association between malnutrition risk and mortality. Considering the competing effects among the clinical endpoints of death with LVAD, heart transplant, and explant due to recovery, cumulative incidence functions (CIFs) were utilized to illustrate the specific hazard function, and their differences were tested by the Fine-Gray test. Adjusting competing risk analysis was also performed. The adjusted factors included age, gender, year of therapy, current implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) therapy, INTERMACS profile 1–2, dialysis, blood urea nitrogen, total bilirubin, history of cardiac surgery, concomitant cardiac surgery, device indication, and modified Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI). The modified CCI was calculated in reference to the previous study [ ]. For variables violating the proportional hazard assumption, extended Cox regressions and competing risk regressions with time-dependent covariates were employed. For secondary outcomes of adverse events, an adjusted competing risk analysis was performed to assess the association of malnutrition risk with time-to-the-first adverse events, accounting for competing events of death, transplant, and explant due to recovery. Finally, the effects of malnutrition risk on QoL and 6MWT that measured in survivors were investigated. Each patient was re-categorized (three groups: no, mild, and moderate to severe malnutrition risk) at each time point according to the calculated GNRI values. Differences in QoL and 6MWT during follow-up were determined by one-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test as appropriate. Estimated effects were expressed as hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) in Cox regression and sub-distribution HRs (SHRs) with 95% CIs in competing-risk regression. A two-tailed p-value of <0.05 was considered significant. Analyses were performed using Stata/MP 17.0 (Stata-Corp, Texas 77845 USA), and R 3.6.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). 3 Results 3.1 Characteristics of patients A total of 5,429 patients with the a mean pre-implant GNRI value of 91.1 who underwent LVAD implantation were included (Figure S1). Patients were divided into three groups according to the pre-implant severity of malnutrition risk indicated by GNRI values before LVAD implantation: moderate to severe (2,708), mild (1,409), and absence of risk (1,312) ( ). The baseline characteristics of included patients are presented in and Table S1. The mean age was 70.2 ± 4.2 years old with 83.7% of male. There were no differences in the terms of the primary diagnosis for HF. Most of the patients (67.8%) used LVAD as the destination therapy. Compared to the group of patients without the malnutrition risk, patients in the group of moderate to severe risk, received more inotrope therapy, mechanical ventilation, and more assist device implantation by either intra‐aortic balloon pumping (IABP) or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) before the LVAD implantation. More patients with New York Heart Association (NYHA) class IV were in the groups with malnutrition risk, and they had more severe INTERMACS profiles. 3.2 Trends in malnutrition risk before and after LVAD

Nevertheless, 37.40% of patients still had a malnutrition risk including mild, and moderate to severe risk, even after one year of LVAD implant and this proportion remained relatively stable until 24 months after the LVAD implantation ( ). 3.3 Pre-implant malnutrition risk and 90-day mortality A significant difference in 90-day mortality was detected by the log-rank test ( P < 0.001, Figure S2a). A competing risk analysis was conducted by calculating the cumulative incidence of death (Figure S2b). Increasing pre-implant malnutrition risk was associated with a significantly high 90-day cumulative incidence of death (P < 0.001). Dose-response analysis via RCS Cox regression showed that the mortality hazard decreased significantly along with reduced malnutrition risk until the GNRI increased to about 102 (Figure S2c). Figure S2d summarizes the adjusted estimates from Cox and competing-risk regressions. After adjusting, patients with pre-implant moderate-to-severe malnutrition risk were associated with a significantly increased risk of 90-day mortality (HR: 1.55; 95% CI: 1.26 to 1.91, P < 0.001). When the GNRI values were considered as continuous variables, increasing the malnutrition risk ( i.e. , decreasing GNRI by 5 points) was associated with an increased risk of death (HR:1.10, 95% CI:1.06–1.15, P < 0.001). This association was also verified by multivariable competing risk regression. 3.4 Pre-implant malnutrition risk and long-term survival The 4-year survival estimate for patients without malnutrition risk was 49.8%, for patients with pre-implant mild risk, it was 44.9%, and for patients with moderate-to-severe risk, it was 40.9%. A significant difference was detected by the log-rank test ( P < 0.001, a). To accurately assess the nutritional status of HF patients, it's also essential to consider factors such as dietary intake, muscle mass, micronutrient levels, and functional status [ ]. Our current study had some limitations. First, our data were obtained retrospectively from a large observational database, thus some data related to medical treatments during the follow-up period may not have been included in the analysis. With regards to laboratory data, although INTERMACS selected the latest values close to a specific time-point, changes in these biochemical data during a short period may not be reflected in the database, potentially causing some bias. In addition, while we accounted for gender bias in the competing risk analysis, there is a significant imbalance in the gender ratio. The reasons for women being a minority among patients receiving advanced surgical heart failure treatments may be multifactoral [ ], and the current study may not be enough to fully understand the complex factors contributing to the gender-based difference. Furthermore, the use of the database also severely restricts the availability of nutritional information. It’s important to note that GNRI is a general risk screening tool and does not account for other factors such as dietary intake, muscle mass, micronutrient levels, and functional status. Therefore, the association of malnutrition risk, as indicated by GNRI, and outcomes should be further investigated in prospective studies, and compared to comprehensive diagnostic assessments if applicable, such as the criteria from the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics/American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (AND/ASPEN), the European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN), and the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM). Thirdly, the data set did not include specific information on nutritional interventions implemented to enhance the nutritional status of patients during the study period. It is thus still unclear whether the correction of malnutrition status by specific intervention may improve the prognosis of such patients. Our findings indicate that malnutrition risk is associated with poor prognosis in advanced heart failure patients aged over 65, highlighting the importance of addressing nutritional needs in this population. Further studies to evaluate the effect of nutrition treatment on these patients may be needed. 5 Conclusion In summary, malnutrition risk identified by GNRI is frequent and associated with increased mortality risk, higher infection, poor QoL, and reduced functional exercise capacity in patients aged 65 and above undergoing LVAD implantation. chunks.content: 1 Introduction Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is performed in pediatric patients to cure a range of malignant and non-malignant diseases ( ). Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in ribosomal protein structural genes, leading to abnormal ribosome biogenesis ( ). It is characterized by congenital bone marrow failure syndrome with isolated erythroid hypoplasia and HSCT is the only curative approach ( ). However, chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD), a late complication, remains a major limitation to long-term survival and quality of life ( , ). Among the diverse manifestations of cGVHD, bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS) represents a particularly severe pulmonary complication, characterized by progressive and largely irreversible airflow obstruction ( ). Studies indicate that the incidence of BOS in children after HSCT is 4.5–8.3% ( , ). However, due to the smaller diameter of children’s airways and the more fragile mucosal barrier function, the disease progresses more rapidly, and the 5-year survival rate is only 45% to 59% ( ). The clinical course of BOS can be markedly exacerbated by the development of air-leak syndrome (ALS). ALS is caused by the “Macklin effect”, starting with increased intra-alveolar pressure, leading to alveolar rupture, air peeling along the bronchovascular sheath, and the spread of interstitial emphysema to the mediastinum ( ). The cumulative incidence of ALS following allo-HSCT is estimated to be between 0.83% and 2.3% ( – ). The onset of ALS is frequently associated with respiratory failure, with mortality rates reported to exceed 60%, resulting in extremely rare cases of successful clinical management ( , ). For patients with BOS refractory to intensified immunosuppression, lung transplantation (LTx) remains the only potentially curative option for end-stage lung disease ( ). While experience with LTx for end-stage BOS after allo-HSCT has gradually accumulated in adults, the pediatric experience is limited ( ). Reports of successful transplantation in children, particularly those with ALS as a high-risk comorbidity, are exceptionally rare. We report a 7-year-old girl with DBA who developed BOS combined with ALS following allo-HSCT and successfully underwent bilateral LTx. To our knowledge, this is the youngest and most comprehensively documented case of its kind reported globally. Through dynamic multimodal monitoring and literature comparison, we analyze the pathophysiological mechanisms of disease progression and optimizing the diagnosis and treatment decisions based on dynamic multimodal monitoring results, new theoretical basis and practical paradigms can be provided for the precise diagnosis and treatment of complex pulmonary complications after HSCT in pediatrics. 2 Case presentation We report a 7-year-old girl with DBA. The patient, diagnosed at one year of age, had developed corticosteroid-refractory disease and remained transfusion-dependent. illustrates the clinical timeline of the patient until December 2025. Before HSCT, chest CT showed no significant abnormalities ( ). And pulmonary function tests showed normal spirometry values (FEV1/FVC: 87%; FEV1: 114% of predicted). She had no contraindications and had indications for allo-HSCT. She accepted matched unrelated donor allo-HSCT on June 11, 2024 as definitive therapy. The myeloablative conditioning regimen comprised busulfan (4.4mg/kg, -8~-7d), cyclophosphamide (30mg/kg, -5~-2d), fludarabine(30mg/m 2 , -6~-2d), and anti-thymocyte immunoglobulin (2.5mg/kg, -5~-2d). A peripheral blood stem cell graft was administered at a CD34 + cell dose of 13.3×10 6 cells/kg. GVHD prophylaxis consisted of cyclosporine A (2.5mg/kg/day, maintain the blood drug concentration between 150ng/ml and 250ng/ml), mycophenolate mofetil (30mg/kg/day), and short-course methotrexate (15mg/m 2 on +1d, and 10mg/m 2 on +3d, +5d, and +11d). Neutrophil and platelet engraftment (neutrophil≥0.5×10 9 /L for 3days and platelet≥20×10 9 /L for 7 days without infusion) were documented on +10d and +11d, respectively. The epithelium of the small bile ducts in the portal areas showed degeneration, and no signs of venulitis in the portal areas or central venous inflammation were observed. Extensive subcutaneous emphysema was observed on the face, neck, and chest, accompanied by a snowball sensation on palpation. On auscultation of the chest, bilateral breath sounds were diminished. These findings were consistent with BO after HSCT ( ). In the early postoperative period, the patient received mechanical ventilation support via orotracheal intubation and was successfully extubated on the 4th postoperative day. However, reintubation was performed on the 6th postoperative day due to respiratory muscle weakness, hypercapnia, and complicated airway hemorrhage. Post-reintubation mechanical ventilation parameters: PCV mode with PIP 17 cmH 2 O, PEEP 5 cmH 2 O, respiratory rate 17 breaths/min, FiO 2 0.55. Meanwhile, anti-GVHD therapy with tacrolimus (0.03mg/kg/day, maintain the blood drug concentration between 7 and 12 ug/L) combined with methylprednisolone (2mg/kg/day) was administered, along with renal replacement therapy and nutritional support. The patient was successfully extubated on the 27th postoperative day and subsequently weaned off oxygen gradually. CT examination showed clear graft morphology without evidence of acute rejection or recurrence of cGVHD ( ). To our knowledge, this child is the youngest case diagnosed with DBA to successfully undergo LTx after developing these complications following allo-HSCT. This case clearly illustrates the progressive sequence of aGVHD, BOS, ALS, and pulmonary function failure, highlighting the limitations of current treatment options. This case offers valuable clinical insight into the pathophysiological progression of chronic pulmonary complications associated with cGVHD. Furthermore, it establishes a clinically actionable framework for managing this high-risk population. Early detection of BOS in pediatric post-HSCT populations remains challenging due to nonspecific initial symptoms and the invasiveness of definitive diagnostic procedures. Early symptoms in pediatric patients are often subtle, commonly presenting as shortness of breath and wheezing after activity, which can easily be confused with pulmonary infections, leading to delays in diagnosis. Importantly, symptoms may not only be minimal but can also be completely absent during the developing phase of BOS, making routine screening even more critical ( , ). Although pathological examination remains the gold standard for the diagnosis of obliterative bronchiolitis, lung biopsy is associated with severe complications including pneumothorax, mediastinal emphysema, persistent air leak syndrome, and even mortality ( , ). This case established a multimodal diagnostic framework integrating dynamic pulmonary function monitoring with HRCT that enabled pre-emptive identification of BOS progression and timely transplantation listing. The core value of dynamic pulmonary function monitoring lies in its ability to provide early warnings based on trend analysis. Prior to HSCT and during the liver GVHD phase, both FEV 1 and the FEV 1 /FVC ratio remained relatively preserved: FEV 1 stayed above the predicted normal range (114% pre-HSCT, 101% at liver GVHD), while FEV 1 /FVC maintained a stable 87% across these two stages. This stability suggests that early post-HSCT complications targeting the liver exert minimal effect on pulmonary mechanics—a observation consistent with reports that liver GVHD and pulmonary complications post-HSCT involve divergent immune-mediated organ targeting ( ). It is worth noting that with the emergence of BOS, both of these indicators experienced a sharp and clinically significant decline: FEV 1 dropped by approximately 63%, falling to 37% of the predicted value; FEV 1 /FVC decreased by about 40%, dropping to 52% of the predicted value. This sharp reduction directly reflects the pathological hallmark of BOS which impairs expiratory airflow and disrupts ventilatory efficiency ( ). A subsequent mild further reduction (to 36% for FEV 1 and 50% for FEV 1 /FVC) in the phrase of BOS combined with infection underscores the synergistic deleterious effect of secondary infections on pre-existing BOS-related airway damage. According to the 2024 ATS guidelines for the diagnosis of BOS after HSCT in children, a “FEV 1 decline rate > 15%” can be used as a warning indicator for BOS ( ). This threshold prompted immediate intervention in our patient despite absolute values not yet meeting formal BOS criteria. The monitoring results of this case verified the clinical value of this warning indicator, suggesting that for children at high risk of cGVHD, dynamic monitoring of the trend of lung function changes is more diagnostically significant than a single measurement. Studies have shown that the diagnostic sensitivity of HRCT for BOS in children is 85% to 90% ( ). Before HSCT, the HRCT of the children showed no significant abnormalities, but typical mosaic perfusion signs and bronchial wall thickening appeared in the BOS stage, which were characteristic imaging manifestations of BOS ( ). When the disease progresses to the ALS stage, HRCT further reveals atelectasis, extensive subcutaneous emphysema, and mediastinal emphysema, thereby visually reflecting the air leakage caused by the destruction of the airway structure. The combined application of HRCT and pulmonary function monitoring in this case successfully avoided diagnostic delays and gained time for early intervention. Importantly, while multimodal monitoring offers a non-invasive diagnostic basis, pathological confirmation remains indispensable for clarifying disease severity and the underlying progression mechanisms—a notion corroborated by pathological examinations of the explanted lung tissue in the present case. The definitive features of obliterative bronchiolitis included bronchiolar luminal stenosis or occlusion caused by submucosal and adventitial fibrosis. These changes explained the irreversible airflow obstruction observed in pulmonary function tests. The concurrent vasculitis, characterized by vascular wall thickening and chronic inflammatory cell infiltration, not only compromised pulmonary microcirculation—potentially worsening epithelial ischemia and fibrosis—but also likely reduced the delivery of immunosuppressive agents to target tissues, leading to treatment resistance ( ). Furthermore, inflammation damaged the bronchovascular sheath, which may have allowed air to leak, causing the extensive subcutaneous and mediastinal emphysema typical of ALS ( ). The multi-dimensional confirmation of HRCT, pulmonary function, and pathology has established a complete evidence chain of “morphology-function-pathology,” providing support for analyzing disease progression mechanisms and optimizing diagnosis and treatment decisions. This extensive lesion, involving the airway, vascular, and interstitial regions, explains the rapid progression of BOS to ALS observed in this case. Children’s unique anatomical vulnerabilities—smaller airway diameters causing disproportionately greater obstruction from equivalent inflammation or fibrosis, incompletely developed elastic fibers, and fragile alveolar walls—amplify these pathological effects and account for the significantly higher ALS risk in pediatric BOS compared to adults ( ). Given this accelerated disease trajectory and the extremely poor prognosis of BOS, minimizing modifiable risk factors should be a priority in pretransplant planning, especially for non-malignant diseases like DBA where the risk-benefit balance differs from malignancies. Key preventive strategies include: conditioning regimen optimization, where reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC) protocols may offer lower pulmonary toxicity compared to busulfan-based myeloablative regimens—although this benefit must be carefully weighed against the increased risk of graft rejection, particularly in the setting of unrelated donor transplantation ( ); GVHD prophylaxis incorporating post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy), which has recently been associated with a reduced incidence of BOS ( ); graft source selection, with bone marrow potentially conferring a lower risk of BOS compared to peripheral blood stem cells ( , ); and respiratory virus prevention strategies, including vaccination administered after immune reconstitution and anti-infection prophylaxis ( ). This case illustrates accelerated disease progression potentially driven by both the busulfan-based myeloablative conditioning and pulmonary infections complicating post-transplant BOS ( , ). Despite GVHD-prophylactic measures—including shortening busulfan exposure to 2 days and administering prophylactic acyclovir and posaconazole following transplantation—GVHD still developed in this patient. This interplay between pathological vulnerabilities and environmental exposures underscores the critical importance of pretransplant risk factor modification and early intervention in high-risk pediatric patients. Glucocorticoids remain the first−line therapy for BOS after HSCT, yet corticosteroid use itself constitutes a critical risk factor for persistent air leak and pneumothorax ( , ). The pathophysiological basis for this paradox lies in corticosteroid-mediated impairment of wound healing and tissue repair mechanisms. Corticosteroids delay alveolar epithelial regeneration, impair collagen synthesis, and reduce tensile strength of healing tissues ( ). In the context of pre-existing lung injury, these effects may transform manageable air leaks into persistent, life-threatening complications. Future therapeutic strategies must address this paradox through targeted approaches that preserve immunosuppressive efficacy while minimizing pulmonary toxicity. The development of steroid-sparing regimens, including JAK inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and extracorporeal photopheresis, offers potential pathways to circumvent this dilemma ( ). When medical therapy fails, as in this case with refractory BOS complicated by ALS and type II respiratory failure, LTx represents the only curative option ( ). Post-HSCT recipients present unique selection considerations that influenced our MDT decision-making. Firstly, a stable donor chimerism, especially complete chimerism, is associated with a reduced risk of GVHD and the establishment of immune tolerance ( ). Preclinical models have demonstrated that stable donor chimerism correlates with improved acceptance of lung allografts in combined lung and bone marrow transplantation ( ). Secondly, several studies have demonstrated that HLA mismatch between lung donors and recipients is a well−established adverse prognostic factor, associated with inferior survival and an increased risk of chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) ( , ). Secondly, several studies have demonstrated that HLA mismatch between lung donors and recipients is a well−established adverse prognostic factor, associated with inferior survival and an increased risk of chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) ( , ). Furthermore, organ size matching poses particular challenges in pediatric LTx. Oversized grafts carry the risk of atelectasis and impaired hemodynamics, whereas undersized grafts may result in residual pleural space and prolonged air leak. In this patient, the prior HSCT was carried out using a fully HLA−matched donor, and complete donor chimerism was confirmed prior to LTx. Following comprehensive evaluation by a MDT and consideration of these favorable factors, the child was expeditiously listed for LTx. Although the donor to recipient pTLC ratio indicated substantial graft oversizing relative to recipient capacity, anatomical compatibility was supported by well-matched thoracic dimensions: chest circumference measured 60 cm in the donor versus 58 cm in the recipient. Consequently, the donor lungs were deemed clinically appropriate for transplantation based on physical dimensional compatibility. Standard LTx recipients typically receive triple-drug maintenance therapy comprising calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs, such as cyclosporine or tacrolimus), glucocorticoids, and a third agent (antiproliferative agents such as azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil) ( ). In contrast, first-line immunosuppressive therapy for cGVHD following HSCT consists of glucocorticoids with or without CNIs ( ). However, no evidence-based guidelines or prospective studies currently exist to inform standardized immunosuppressive management in this unique population with pre-existing cGVHD undergoing LTx. This therapeutic gap necessitates individualized strategies that must achieve precise equilibrium among three competing therapeutic objectives: prevention of lung allograft rejection, control of underlying cGVHD disease activity, and mitigation of substantially elevated infectious risk attributable to overlapping immunosuppression ( ). For HSCT recipients with prior CNI-induced nephrotoxicity, a once-daily cyclosporine regimen may be adopted post-LTx, with dose individualization guided by area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) monitoring and lower target trough concentrations (e.g., 100–150 ng/mL during the first postoperative month) to preserve residual renal function ( ). In summary, HSCT recipients with cGVHD undergoing LTx require highly individualized immunosuppressive modifications built upon standard LTx protocols, with careful consideration of pre-existing cGVHD organ involvement patterns, prior immunosuppressive drug exposure history, and the dynamic interplay between rejection and infectious risks following LTx ( , ). This case report has several limitations. First, diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLco) and static lung volume testing (including total lung capacity [TLC] and residual volume [RV]) were not performed due to technical limitations and patient cooperation issues in this pediatric setting. These parameters could have provided earlier detection of small airway dysfunction and air trapping before the significant FEV1 decline, potentially enabling earlier intervention ( , ). Second, the single-case nature limits generalizability, and prospective studies are needed to validate the monitoring and treatment strategies described. Third, long-term follow-up after LTx is ongoing, and late complications including chronic lung allograft dysfunction require continued surveillance. 4 Conclusion This report describes the successful sequential bilateral LTx in a 7-year-old girl with DBA who developed refractory BOS complicated by ALS after allo-HSCT. Dynamic multimodal monitoring, including serial pulmonary function tests and HRCT, enables early detection of BOS. Pathological examination clarifies the BOS to ALS progression mechanism related to pediatric-specific vulnerabilities. MDT collaboration and recognizing ALS as a “transplant warning signal” ensure timely curative transplantation. The refractory nature of the disease underscores the need for early intervention in high-risk patients. LTx has proven effective, but long-term follow-up and further research on early warning and prophylactic strategies are needed to improve outcomes of complex post-HSCT pulmonary complications in pediatrics.

ILD patients exhibit diaphragmatic structural and functional abnormalities (thickening, reduced contractility/excursion, increased activation) that correlate with disease severity. What is known and what is new? • The dyspnea experienced by patients with ILD is partly attributable to diaphragmatic dysfunction. However, similar studies using ultrasound to assess diaphragmatic function in patients with ILD remain scarce. Tissue Doppler imaging (TDI) has not yet been applied to the quantitative assessment of diaphragmatic motion in this patient population. • This study is the first to use TDI for diaphragmatic motion assessment in ILD, detecting ILD-related diaphragmatic changes compared with healthy controls. Diaphragmatic ultrasound parameters in ILD patients correlate with several clinical indicators, including pulmonary function test results, St George’s Respiratory Questionnaire scores, and modified Medical Research Council Dyspnoea Scale grades. What is the implication, and what should change now? • As a non-invasive, simple tool, diaphragmatic ultrasound parameters correlate with clinical indicators of ILD severity, which may indirectly reflect patients’ respiratory function. Its clinical utility for guiding drug interventions or pulmonary rehabilitation requires prospective validation with larger cohorts. Introduction Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a restrictive pulmonary disease characterized by impaired lung expansion and reduced total lung capacity (TLC) ( ). Most patients with ILD present with predominant clinical manifestations, including cough, progressively worsening dyspnoea, impaired lung function, and reduced exercise tolerance ( ). Recent research has demonstrated that dyspnoea and impaired exercise capacity in these patients are at least partially associated with respiratory muscle dysfunction—particularly dysfunction of the diaphragm ( , ). The diaphragm, the primary inspiratory muscle, accounts for 60–80% of respiratory work at rest. Diaphragm elevation causes traction in restrictive lung disease. This elevation induces diaphragmatic overload, ultimately leading to diaphragmatic fatigue and dyspnoea ( , ). Concurrently, multiple factors in patients with ILD—including hypoxaemia, systemic inflammation, glucocorticoid use, reduced physical activity, and malnutrition—further impair diaphragmatic structure and function ( ). Evaluating diaphragm function is crucial for ILD patients. Current methods for assessing diaphragmatic function primarily include transdiaphragmatic pressure (Pdi) measurement, electrophysiological testing, chest X-ray, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasound. Transdiaphragmatic pressure is considered the gold standard for evaluating diaphragmatic function; however, its invasiveness and operational complexity limit its clinical applicability. Electrophysiological testing is also invasive and requires high technical expertise. Chest X-ray and CT involve ionizing radiation, precluding short-term repeated use. In contrast, diaphragmatic ultrasound is a radiation-free, easy-to-perform, and readily repeatable assessment tool that enables real-time dynamic visualization of diaphragmatic motion. Currently, B-mode and M-mode ultrasound are commonly used to evaluate diaphragmatic thickness and mobility, and these modalities have been widely applied in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and critically ill individuals in recent years ( ). Previous research has shown that diaphragmatic mobility is altered in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (a subtype of ILD) compared with healthy individuals, and this alteration strongly correlates with pulmonary function parameters and clinical indicators (e.g., the 6-minute walk test) ( ). However, diaphragmatic motion characteristics in the broader population of patients with ILD have not been fully characterized. Tissue Doppler imaging (TDI) is an ultrasonic technique designed to assess tissue motion, which is widely used in echocardiographic evaluation of cardiac function. The TDI curve is a velocity-time waveform that allows quantification of diaphragmatic velocity and acceleration during contraction and relaxation. Previously, Soilemezi et al. used TDI to demonstrate that peak diaphragmatic contraction velocity in critically ill patients correlates with Pdi and the pressure-time product across the diaphragm (PTPdi; a marker of diaphragmatic respiratory drive) ( ). However, similar studies using ultrasound to assess diaphragmatic function in patients with ILD remain scarce. TDI has not yet been applied to the quantitative assessment of diaphragmatic motion in this patient population. The present study aims to quantitatively evaluate diaphragmatic function in patients with ILD using multimodal ultrasound (including B-mode, M-mode, and TDI). This approach provides a more comprehensive understanding of diaphragmatic characteristics in patients with ILD, while further analyzing the correlations between diaphragmatic ultrasound parameters and clinical features of ILD. Ultimately, this study seeks to provide theoretical support for the application of diaphragmatic ultrasound in rehabilitation management and disease monitoring for patients with ILD. Methods Study design and subjects This study was a prospective observational study. Forty-four patients with ILD and 31 healthy volunteers were consecutively enrolled between December 2024 and July 2025 at the Department of Respiratory Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University. Patient inclusion criteria: age >18 years, fulfilling current American Thoracic Society (ATS)/European Respiratory Society (ERS)/Japanese Respiratory Society (JRS)/Latin American Thoracic Association (ALAT) guideline criteria ( ), and clinically diagnosed with ILD based on clinical presentation, pulmonary function tests (PFTs), chest CT, and histological examination. Patient exclusion criteria included: existing complications such as obstructive ventilatory dysfunction (e.g., COPD), active infection, history of upper abdominal or thoracic surgery (except for ILD biopsy diagnosis), neuromuscular disease, or inability to cooperate with examinations. Healthy volunteer inclusion criteria: age >18 years, absence of any cardiopulmonary or neuromuscular disease, no history of thoracic/upper abdominal surgery, and normal PFT results. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University (No. ES-2025-151-01). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments and the relevant guidelines and regulations of the aforementioned Ethics Committee. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to enrollment (consistent with the committee’s requirements for prospective observational studies). Clinical data collection Baseline data of all participants were extracted from the electronic medical records system of The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University. The extracted data included three categories: (I) demographic and anthropometric data: age, sex, and body mass index (BMI); (II) clinical characteristics: clinical manifestations, disease duration, smoking history, oxygen therapy status, detailed treatment regimens (e.g., antifibrotic agents, glucocorticoids), and comorbidities; (III) functional, symptomatic, and laboratory assessments: results of PFTs, scores of the St George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) and modified Medical Research Council Dyspnoea Scale (mMRC), and serum levels of Krebs von der Lungen 6 (KL-6). Diaphragmatic ultrasound measurements All diaphragmatic ultrasound measurements were performed using an ultrasound system (Resona 9, Mindray Medical International, Shenzhen, China) equipped with three probes: a convex array probe (SC6-1, 1–6 MHz), a linear array probe (L14-3WU, 3–14 MHz), and a phased array probe (SP5-1U, 1–5 MHz). All diaphragmatic ultrasound measurements were performed by a single experienced sonographer who was blinded to the grouping status (ILD patients vs. healthy controls) of all subjects, so as to minimize subjective operational bias induced by prior knowledge of group allocation. To ensure data accuracy, ultrasound images were acquired over at least three consecutive respiratory cycles, and the mean value of three repeated measurements was recorded for each parameter. For the assessment of intra-operator repeatability, the same sonographer conducted repeated measurements of all diaphragmatic ultrasound parameters for all 77 subjects at the same examination session with a 10-minute interval between the two measurement sets, with all measurement procedures strictly consistent with the first round to avoid additional variability. All participants (both ILD patients and healthy volunteers) maintained a supine position during the examination and breathed spontaneously without artificial ventilation. Notably, left diaphragmatic imaging is frequently obscured by gastric and intestinal gas, which compromises image quality and measurement reliability. Therefore, diaphragmatic measurements in this study were confined to the right hemidiaphragm. Deep breathing (DB) was defined as a full respiratory cycle of maximal voluntary inspiration followed by slow, complete expiration for healthy controls. For ILD patients, DB was modified to comfortable maximal DB to avoid respiratory distress induced by forced breathing. All DB measurements were performed in a supine position. Prior to formal measurement, the same sonographer provided 2–3 standardized DB demonstrations and training for all subjects until consistent performance was achieved. For data acquisition, 3 consecutive valid DB cycles with uniform excursion amplitude and cycle duration were recorded for each subject; cycles with abnormal amplitude or incomplete expiration were discarded and repeated. The mean value of the 3 valid cycles was used for statistical analysis. Breathing effort was monitored via combined subjective and objective approaches: the sonographer provided real-time verbal guidance to confirm consistent effort and simultaneously monitored the diaphragmatic motion curve by M-mode ultrasound to ensure uniform effort for all included cycles. No subjects were excluded due to irregular DB performance or poor cooperation, and all DB-related measurement data were complete. On two-dimensional ultrasound images, the diaphragm appeared as a hypoechoic muscular layer sandwiched between the hyperechoic pleural and peritoneal membranes, with a linear hyperechoic band at its center. Diaphragm thickness (DT) and thickening fraction (TF) The 3–14 MHz linear array probe (L14-3WU) was placed at the costophrenic angle between the 8th and 10th ribs along the right mid-axillary line. On two-dimensional ultrasound images, the diaphragm appeared as a hypoechoic muscular layer sandwiched between the hyperechoic pleural and peritoneal membranes, with a linear hyperechoic band at its center. DT was defined as the vertical distance between the pleural and peritoneal layers. Measurements were performed at two time points: quiet breathing (QB) at end-expiration and DB at end-inspiration. To ensure reliability, three consecutive measurements were obtained at each time point, and the mean value was recorded as the final DT. TF was calculated using the formula ( ): TF = [DT-DB − DT-QB]/DT-QB × 100% ( ). Diaphragm excursion (DE) The 1–6 MHz convex array probe (SC6-1) was positioned at the lower margin of the costal arch along the right midclavicular line, angled medially and cephalad. The liver was used as an acoustic window to visualize the diaphragm, which appeared as a hyperechoic linear structure covering the liver surface. M-mode ultrasound was activated to record the real-time movement curve of the diaphragm. Participants were instructed to perform QB and DB sequentially. DE was defined as the maximum vertical distance from the peak of the movement curve (end-inspiration) to the baseline (end-expiration). Three independent DE measurements were taken for each breathing pattern, and the mean value was used for analysis ( ). Diaphragmatic peak velocity and acceleration (TDI mode) The 1–5 MHz phased array probe (SP5-1U) was placed at the same location as DE measurement (right midclavicular line at the lower margin of the costal arch) to identify the hyperechoic structure at the diaphragmatic dome. TDI mode was enabled, with the sampling volume adjusted to 30 mm to cover the full range of diaphragmatic motion and the scan speed set to 25 mm/s. For TDI measurements, real-time TDI mode guidance was applied to calibrate the probe insonation angle at 0° relative to the diaphragmatic movement direction. The subcostal margin at the right midclavicular line was used as the unified acoustic window for all subjects, with the probe position fixed to avoid operational bias. Prior to formal measurement, ultrasonic assessment of diaphragmatic morphology and position was performed for each subject; adaptive fine-tuning of probe position and angle was conducted for ILD patients with abnormal diaphragmatic morphology or position to optimize visualization. TDI image quality screening criteria were strictly followed: only images with clear diaphragmatic motion curves were included for subsequent statistical analysis, and ambiguous or unqualified images were discarded and the measurement repeated. TDI curves were acquired during QB. From the velocity-time curve, two parameters were measured: peak contraction velocity (PCV): maximum velocity during diaphragmatic contraction (upward movement); peak relaxation velocity (PRV): maximum velocity during diaphragmatic relaxation (downward movement). Diaphragmatic acceleration was calculated as the slope of the steepest segment of the TDI curve during both contraction and relaxation ( ). For each parameter, three repeated measurements were averaged ( ). Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 25.0 software. Normally distributed continuous data were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Non-normally distributed continuous data were presented as median [interquartile range (IQR)]. Categorical variables were presented as frequency (percentage). For categorical variables: comparisons were conducted using the Chi-squared test; Fisher’s exact test was used if the expected frequency of any cell was <5. For continuous variables: independent samples t-test was employed for normally distributed data, while Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-normally distributed data. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) (two-way mixed-effects model, absolute agreement) was used to quantitatively evaluate the intra-operator repeatability of all diaphragmatic ultrasound parameters, with ICC values interpreted as follows: <0.50 (poor consistency), 0.50–0.74 (moderate consistency), 0.75–0.89 (good consistency), and ≥0.90 (excellent consistency). Bland-Altman analysis was further performed to assess the measurement agreement and systematic bias between the two rounds of repeated measurements: the mean bias (difference between the first and second measurements) and 95% limits of agreement (95% LoA; mean bias ± 1.96 × SD of the differences) were calculated, and the number and proportion of outlying points outside the 95% LoA were counted for each parameter. To address potential confounding factors (age, sex, steroid use and disease duration) and explore whether steroid use mediates the effect of ILD on diaphragmatic mechanics, multivariate linear regression analyses were performed. Key diaphragmatic parameters were used as dependent variables separately. The independent variables included: (I) core exposure: ILD status (1= ILD patient, 0= healthy control); (II) potential confounders: age, sex, steroid use, and disease duration. The core exposure was forced into the model, while confounders were included via stepwise selection (entry criterion: P<0.05, removal criterion: P>0.10). No significant differences were observed in age, sex, or BMI between the ILD group and the control group (all P>0.05). Among the ILD patients, connective tissue disease-related interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD) was the most prevalent subtype. High-resolution CT imaging mainly showed interstitial infiltration in the bilateral lower lobes. Detailed demographic and baseline characteristics of the two groups are summarized in . Diaphragm measurements All diaphragmatic ultrasound data related to DB were complete for all subjects, with no cases excluded due to non-standard DB maneuver or poor cooperation. Diaphragmatic ultrasound parameters of the two groups are summarized in . During QB, DT was significantly greater in the ILD group than in the healthy control group (P=0.004). In contrast, during DB, DT was significantly lower in the ILD group (P=0.003). The TF of ILD patients was significantly reduced compared with healthy controls (P<0.001). Diaphragm mobility during DB was significantly decreased in the ILD group relative to the control group (P<0.001). No significant difference in DE during QB was observed between the two groups (P=0.87). In the ILD group, TDI revealed significantly higher PRV (P=0.02), contraction acceleration (P=0.02), and relaxation acceleration (P<0.001) compared with healthy controls. There was no significant intergroup difference in PCV during QB (P=0.08). Intra-operator repeatability of diaphragmatic ultrasound parameters Intra-operator repeatability analysis (ICC and Bland-Altman) for all diaphragmatic ultrasound parameters (77 subjects) is detailed in . All parameters exhibited excellent intra-operator consistency (ICC >0.90, all P<0.001). Bland-Altman analysis further confirmed no significant systematic bias across all measurements; a small number of scattered outlying points were observed outside the 95% LoA: DB excursion 6 points (7.8%, 6/77), TF 4 points (5.2%, 4/77), QB excursion 3 points (3.9%, 3/77), contraction acceleration 4 points (5.2%, 4/77), and PRV/relaxation acceleration 2 points each (2.6%, 2/77). The low and clinically acceptable proportion of outlying points, combined with excellent ICC values, validated the high intra-operator repeatability and accuracy of the standardized diaphragmatic ultrasound measurements in this study. Multivariate linear regression analysis To control for potential confounding factors and verify the independent effect of ILD status on diaphragmatic parameters, multivariate linear regression analyses were performed ( ). After adjusting for age, sex, steroid use, and disease duration, ILD status remained an independent factor associated with key diaphragmatic parameters: DT-QB [standardized β =0.33; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.01 to 0.06; P=0.004], DT-DB (standardized β =−0.32; 95% CI: −0.13 to −0.02; P=0.006), TF (standardized β =−0.60; 95% CI: −0.99 to −0.52; P<0.001), DE-DB (standardized β =−0.71; 95% CI: −3.62 to −2.26; P<0.001), PRV (standardized β =0.33; 95% CI: 0.15 to 0.77; P=0.004), contraction acceleration (standardized β =0.32; 95% CI: 0.52 to 2.95; P=0.006), relaxation acceleration (standardized β =0.35; 95% CI: 1.14 to 4.99; P=0.002). Discussion This study used multimodal ultrasound (B-mode, M-mode, TDI) to systematically evaluate diaphragmatic motion in patients with ILD. Key findings: (I) compared with healthy controls, ILD patients showed resting diaphragmatic thickening, reduced TF and DE-DB, plus elevated PRV and motion acceleration; (II) decreased TF/DE and increased acceleration correlated with poorer health-related quality of life (higher SGRQ scores), more severe dyspnea (higher mMRC grades), elevated KL-6 levels, and impaired pulmonary function (reduced FVC, TLC, DLCO). To our knowledge, this is the first study applying TDI for quantitative assessment of diaphragmatic motion in ILD. Our findings expand understanding of ILD-related diaphragmatic pathophysiology and provide a reliable reference for clinical assessment of these patients. In our study, ILD patients exhibited significantly thicker DT at rest but reduced DT, DE, and TF during deep inspiration compared with healthy controls—consistent with previous findings ( , ). As a restrictive pulmonary disorder, ILD is characterized by decreased lung compliance and volume, which elevate the diaphragm cephalad, increase diaphragmatic tension, and limit motion range, resulting in impaired diaphragmatic mobility relative to healthy individuals. This aligns with MRI-based observations of diaphragmatic motion in IPF patients by Yang et al. ( ). Long-term diaphragmatic overload in ILD may induce both fatigue and a “training effect” ( ), leading to compensatory muscle hypertrophy. Combined with systemic factors contributing to diaphragmatic dysfunction, this explains our finding of increased resting DT but reduced contractile function in ILD patients. Notably, our results contradict those of Milesi et al. ( ), who reported lower resting DT in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis patients than in healthy individuals. This discrepancy may stem from more advanced disease in their cohort: end-stage ILD patients may progress to diaphragmatic decompensation and atrophy with disease chronicity and severity. TDI—a well-established technique for assessing myocardial systolic and diastolic function—accurately captures low-velocity, high-frequency tissue motion. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply TDI for evaluating diaphragmatic motion in ILD patients, providing TDI curves, peak contraction/relaxation velocities, and acceleration data as a reference for future research. Notably, strict quality control protocols were implemented for TDI measurements, including real-time mode-guided probe angle calibration, a unified acoustic window with fixed probe position, pre-measurement diaphragmatic morphology/position assessment with adaptive probe adjustment for ILD patients, and standardized image quality screening. These measures effectively eliminated TDI measurement errors caused by probe angulation deviation and intergroup differences in diaphragmatic morphology and position between ILD patients and healthy controls, thus ensuring the accuracy and reliability of all TDI-derived measurement results. Key TDI findings included significantly higher PRV, systolic acceleration, and relaxation acceleration in ILD patients versus healthy controls. Dyspnea in restrictive lung diseases like ILD is largely driven by increased neural respiratory drive, a consequence of pathological high lung elastic resistance and neuromechanical inefficiency ( , ). ILD patients face elevated inspiratory muscle loads but fail to achieve adequate tidal volume, potentially compensating by increasing respiratory rate—one plausible mechanism for enhanced diaphragmatic motion velocity. This aligns with Soilemezi et al. ( ), who linked diaphragmatic PCV to Pdi and respiratory drive, noting rapid relaxation as a fatigue-mitigating compensatory response. While ILD patients had numerically higher peak systolic velocity, this did not reach statistical significance (P=0.083), likely due to our small sample size. The elevated contraction/relaxation acceleration observed in ILD patients likely reflects increased respiratory drive as a compensatory response to impaired lung function and dyspnea, whereas velocity alone would only capture the magnitude of diaphragmatic motion without accounting for the effort required to generate that motion. This explains why acceleration parameters showed stronger correlations with clinical markers of disease severity (SGRQ scores, mMRC grades) than velocity alone, highlighting the added value of acceleration in assessing diaphragmatic adaptive changes in ILD. Our multivariate linear regression analyses further confirmed that ILD status is an independent driver of diaphragmatic structural and functional abnormalities, even after adjusting for potential confounding factors (age, sex, steroid use and disease duration).
